content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In Christian teaching, 'worship' most commonly signifies reverent adoration, homage, and self-surrender directed exclusively to God — the act of ascribing supreme worth ('worth-ship') to God, expressed outwardly in bowing down or prostration (Hebrew shachah, Greek proskuneo, literally 'to bow/kiss toward') and inwardly in submission of the whole self. It symbolizes the creature's acknowledgment of the Creator's absolute worthiness, glory, and lordship, and by extension the total orientation of one's life toward God rather than idols or rivals.","primary_basis":["Exodus 20:3-5 (worship reserved for God alone; prohibition of idols)","Deuteronomy 6:13 (fear the LORD your God and serve him only)","Matthew 4:10 / Luke 4:8 (Jesus: 'Worship the Lord your God, and serve him only')","John 4:23-24 (true worshipers worship the Father in spirit and truth)","Psalm 95:6 ('Come, let us bow down in worship, let us kneel before the LORD our Maker')","Psalm 29:2 / Psalm 96:9 (ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship in the splendor of holiness)","Romans 12:1 (offer your bodies as a living sacrifice — your spiritual/reasonable worship)","Revelation 4:10-11 and 5:12-14 (heavenly worship: 'Worthy is the Lamb')","Revelation 22:8-9 (angel refuses worship: 'Worship God!')","Hebrews 12:28 (worship God acceptably with reverence and awe)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Worship as whole-life obedience and service rather than a cultic or ritual act — every act of life offered to God constitutes worship (the 'all of life is worship' reading, emphasized in evangelical and Reformed teaching).","basis":["Romans 12:1-2","Deuteronomy 10:12-13","Micah 6:6-8","Colossians 3:17","1 Corinthians 10:31"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Worship as the corporate, liturgical, and sacramental assembly of the church — the gathered congregation's ordered praise, word, and sacrament (Eucharist/Lord's Supper), central in Catholic, Orthodox, and liturgical Protestant traditions.","basis":["Acts 2:42-47","Hebrews 10:24-25","1 Corinthians 11:23-26","Colossians 3:16","Acts 13:2"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Worship as sacrifice of praise — the replacement of Old Testament animal sacrifice with verbal/musical praise and thanksgiving offered through Christ.","basis":["Hebrews 13:15-16","Psalm 50:14, 23","Psalm 141:2","1 Peter 2:5"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Worship as experiential encounter with God's manifest presence — the charismatic/Pentecostal emphasis that worship (especially sung praise) ushers worshipers into intimacy with God, sometimes tied to the idea that God 'inhabits the praises' of his people.","basis":["Psalm 22:3","John 4:23-24","2 Chronicles 5:13-14","Psalm 100"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Worship as covenant renewal — a structured dialogical drama in which God calls, cleanses, instructs, feeds, and sends his people, re-enacting the covenant relationship (a reading in Reformed liturgical theology).","basis":["Exodus 24:1-11","Nehemiah 8-9","Isaiah 6:1-8 (as a pattern of call, confession, cleansing, commission)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Worship narrowly identified with music and singing — a popular contemporary usage ('worship' = the song portion of a service); widely used colloquially but generally criticized by scholars as a reduction of the biblical concept.","basis":["Psalm 96:1-2","Ephesians 5:19","Colossians 3:16"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Worship defined etymologically as 'worth-ship' — ascribing worth or worthiness to God as its essential core (a definitional emphasis found across popular and academic treatments, e.g., following writers like Evelyn Underhill).","basis":["Revelation 4:11","Revelation 5:12","Psalm 29:1-2"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"'Worship' is less a symbol than a foundational biblical practice and theological category, so its 'symbolic meaning' is usually framed as what the act signifies: exclusive allegiance, homage, and total self-offering to God. There is broad ecumenical consensus on this core (worship = reverent adoration and submission due to God alone), grounded in the Hebrew shachah (to bow down) and Greek proskuneo (to prostrate/do homage) plus latreuo (to serve). The main interpretive divergences concern scope and emphasis — ritual/liturgical act vs. whole-life orientation vs. experiential encounter — rather than the core meaning. John 4:23-24 ('in spirit and truth') is the most contested proof text, read variously as inward sincerity plus doctrinal truth, worship enabled by the Holy Spirit, or worship centered on Christ as the truth. The New Testament application of worship language to Jesus (Matthew 28:9, 17; Hebrews 1:6; Revelation 5) is also standardly cited in Christological arguments, since worship is reserved for God alone."}
